column3: Its wish not to have received the record supplies a closely related voice of regret after irreversible loss, though in the judgment scene.
The unalterable revealed word and the absence of refuge apart from God frame the collapse that drives the owner back to his Lord.
It repeats the image of a place fallen on its trellises and demonstrates God's power to restore life after devastation.
Destroyed unjust towns left fallen on their trellises give a near-exact image of collapse joined to moral wrongdoing.
The later surah scene has alleged partners summoned but unable to answer, directly extending the owner's repudiation of association after loss.
It explicitly disavows associating other gods with God, supplying the theological opposite of the owner's belated confession.
The wrongdoer's hand-biting and wish for a different path closely parallel the focus's physical regret and retrospective repudiation.
Its warning against pursuing worldly adornment supplies the local moral setting for the garden owner's attachment to his wealth.
Homes left empty because of their wrongdoing parallel the focus's ruined, emptied garden and make the moral dimension explicit.
The disbeliever's wish to have been dust offers an eschatological counterpart to the owner's regret after his illusion collapses.
It opens the two-garden parable and establishes the created prosperity whose destruction the focus narrates.
Its warning that association with God is an enormous unforgiven sin clarifies the gravity of the owner's final renunciation.
The companion's statement, "I do not associate anyone with my Lord," is the direct positive counterpart to the owner's final regret.
The nearby warning that Fire will surround wrongdoers supplies the moral consequence that frames the parable's destructive reversal.
The legal distribution of inheritance uses partnership language in an unrelated technical sense.
The wish to have prepared for one's true life is a related expression of regret, but it does not illuminate the garden's collapse or association.
The abundant yield and river explain the material flourishing that is suddenly encompassed and lost in the focus.
God's exclusive governance and the statement that He shares His judgment with no one support the focus's rejection of association.
Cain's becoming regretful after wrongdoing offers a moral parallel to the owner's regret after the consequence of his error appears.
The local promise not to waste the reward of good work contrasts with the owner's futile expenditure on a possession that collapses.
At the gathering, those who associated partners are asked where their supposed partners are, directly clarifying the futility the owner recognizes.
The declaration of calling only on the Lord and associating no one with Him directly supplies the faithfulness missing from the owner's earlier stance.
The companion explicitly predicts that the garden may become bare, slippery ground, immediately anticipating the destruction in the focus.
The question, "Where are those you used to associate?" gives an afterlife counterpart to the owner's renunciation of association.
The image of hollow palm trunks has only a distant visual resemblance to the garden's ruined supports.
The enduring gardens granted as reward contrast with the temporary worldly garden whose owner thought it secure.
It exposes claims that powerless beings are intercessors and rejects the partners people associate with God, directly clarifying the focus's confession.
God's delayed seizure of unjust towns offers a broader pattern in which apparent security ends in divine taking.
The predicted loss of the garden's water immediately supplies the mechanism of irreversible loss realized in the focus.
Joseph's refusal to associate anything with God gives a direct theological contrast to the owner's late repentance.
Cain's murder and becoming a loser do not materially clarify the ruined garden, regret, or association in the focus.
The owner's boast in fruits, wealth, and followers immediately explains what he has spent on and now sees destroyed.
Sharing punishment does not clarify the focus beyond an incidental root match.
The hypocrite's wish to have shared military success is unrelated to the owner's loss and theological regret.
The companion corrects the owner's entrance into his garden by attributing its existence and power to God.
Moses asking that Aaron share his task uses association in an unrelated sense.
The description of Hell boiling does not clarify the focus's collapse, regret, or association.
The immediate preceding claim that the garden would never perish is overturned by its actual destruction in the focus.
The associates' false denial that they associated partners forms a contrast to the owner's eventual candid recognition.
Moses seeking refuge from stoning has no focused connection to the garden owner.
The next ayah shows that the owner has neither a rescuing group nor self-help after the loss, completing the focus's reversal.
In distress people forget what they associated with God, a related pattern of collapse exposing the inadequacy of association.
God is named as the creator of trellised gardens and their fruit, correcting the owner's possessive treatment of his productive garden.
The owner's doubt about the Hour and presumption of a better return immediately contextualize the repentance voiced after his garden's loss.
Abraham's repudiation of association after the setting of transient celestial bodies supplies a related correction to reliance on what passes away.
The following parable of vegetation becoming scattered debris generalizes the same rapid collapse of worldly growth.
The parable concludes that true authority, best reward, and best outcome belong to God, resolving the owner's misplaced confidence.
The statement that people would not have associated had God willed is only a broad doctrinal connection.
Moses's fear in the city is unrelated to the garden owner's loss and confession.
The companion identifies the owner's position as disbelief in his Creator, providing the direct diagnosis behind his final repentance.
Its general rejection of association supplies only a distant theological parallel.
The image of hands stretched toward unreachable water closely complements the owner's turning hands over a loss and exposes futile reliance apart from God.
God as sole protector and sustainer, joined with a command not to associate, corrects the owner's misplaced dependence on possessions.
Moses's refuge in the Lord from one who rejects the Day of Account supplies a judgment-oriented contrast to the owner's earlier self-assurance.
Shared punishment after wrongdoing is only a broad consequence parallel and does not specifically clarify the owner's regret.
On the Day of Resurrection God asks about the partners people contended for, directly paralleling the focus's late repudiation.
It states that association nullifies deeds and makes one a loser, sharpening the significance of the owner's ruined investment and confession.
The believers' request for a surah and the hypocrites' fear of fighting do not clarify the focus.
The promise that true religion will prevail is not a focused neighbour of the garden collapse.
God's alternation of night and day does not materially illuminate the owner's turning hands or the garden's fall.
After the sun sets, Abraham repudiates association, providing a close corrective to treating a passing visible thing as lordly support.
Those who relied on a hidden calculation become regretful when events reverse, a meaningful pattern alongside the owner's sudden remorse.
The believers' defining refusal to associate anything with their Lord directly contrasts with the owner's final admission.
The promised garden with rivers and fruits is a broad contrast to the owner's perishable worldly garden.
It rejects the alleged partners attached to God and asserts His exclusive might and wisdom, supporting the focus's rejection of association.
The command to worship God alone and the declaration that return is to Him directly answer the owner's final appeal to his Lord.
The command to Abraham not to associate anything with God supplies a direct theological corrective, though in the setting of the House.
Sin encompassing a person before entry into the Fire gives a consequential counterpart to the garden being encompassed and the owner's realization.
The challenge that alleged partners cannot originate or restore creation establishes God's exclusive power over what the owner treated as secure.
The description of desert Arabs' disbelief and ignorance of limits does not clarify the focus.
It challenges associating beings that create nothing and are themselves created, directly undercutting every nondivine object of reliance.
Moses's reminder of Israel's blessings is not sufficiently tied to the garden owner's collapse or association.
The believer explicitly refuses to associate with God what he has no knowledge of and calls instead to the Mighty Forgiving One.
The inherited-association excuse has only a distant relation to the owner's personal recognition of association.
It portrays association with God as a catastrophic fall, a vivid theological counterpart to the garden owner's collapse and regret.
The human question denying post-death life parallels the owner's earlier doubt about the Hour in the immediate preceding ayah.
Those who associated partners find no intercessors and disavow them, directly extending the focus's repudiation after loss.
The etiquette of entering unoccupied houses is unrelated to the focus.
It warns that association would nullify deeds, making the owner's remorse over his lost outlay morally substantive.
The encompassing punishment scene is only a general consequence parallel, without a focused link to the garden or association.
It questions how people can feel secure while associating without authority, directly challenging the owner's earlier security in false supports.
The severe taking of unjust towns offers a broader pattern of sudden loss overtaking those who wrong themselves.
It identifies a form of belief mixed with association, helping explain how the owner can invoke his Lord yet confess association only after collapse.
Its comparison of charitable spending before and after victory has only a remote overlap through expenditure.
The question whether God is better than what people associate with Him supplies a concise theological corrective to the owner's former reliance.
The hypocrites' refusal to come to revelation and the Messenger is not a focused parallel.
It says those who invoke partners follow only conjecture, directly matching the owner's former unsupported confidence and association.
The treaty exception for certain polytheists is unrelated to the focus.
The Day of Gathering separates people from their alleged partners, directly clarifying the final rejection of association.
The believers' reverence, patience, prayer, and charity offer only a broad constructive contrast to the owner.
The revival of dead earth by rain displays God's power over life and loss, offering a broad corrective to despair before ruined land.
The statement that grain grows does not materially clarify the focus.
Satan disavows being associated with God and tells wrongdoers to blame themselves, closely illuminating the owner's self-reproach and renunciation.
The extended ruling on sorcery and its harm does not clarify the garden owner's regret or association.
The hypocrites' presumptuous question about punishment is only a distant contrast to remorse after consequence.
The closing greeting to the messengers has no focused connection.
The promise to faithful worshippers who associate nothing with God provides a constructive contrast to the owner's belated confession.
The rules on an indirect marriage proposal are unrelated to the focus.
The detailed pilgrimage rules are unrelated to the focus.
God's instruction to Moses and Aaron to go with signs does not clarify the garden owner's loss or repentance.
The local declaration that wealth and children are worldly adornment while lasting righteous deeds are better directly corrects the owner's lost investment and former valuation.
The gathering before the Lord with no one left behind supplies the return-to-God horizon behind the owner's belated confession.
The record of deeds produces an explicit cry of regret and exhaustive accounting, illuminating the owner's self-reproach after his loss.
The criminals' certainty that they will fall into the Fire and find no escape extends the parable's exposure of failed security.
Turning from divine signs while forgetting what one's hands have sent ahead gives a moral counterpart to turning his hands over what he spent.
God's mercy and delayed punishment, followed by an appointed term, frame the owner's collapse as neither autonomous nor beyond divine timing.
God destroyed unjust towns and set an appointed time for their destruction, giving a direct broader precedent for the garden's ruin.
A garden of palms and vines destroyed by a fiery whirlwind gives a close material counterpart to the focus's devastated productive garden.
The worldly spending of people who wrong themselves is compared to a wind that destroys their harvest, closely joining ruined produce, expenditure, and self-wronging.
Those facing the Fire wish they could return and act differently, an eschatological counterpart to the owner's wish that he had not associated anyone with his Lord.
When people rejoice in what they have been given, God seizes them suddenly and they become despairing, closely paralleling the reversal of garden prosperity.
Satan's lure through immortality and an undying kingdom supplies a close pattern of being seduced by a promise of permanence.
Those who spend wealth against God's way will find that spending a regret before being overcome, directly echoing the owner's grief over what he spent.
The parable of luxuriant earth thought to be under human control becoming stubble by divine command is a close analogue to the garden's sudden collapse.
Prosperity after hardship makes a person boast that misfortunes have gone, a character pattern behind the owner's misplaced security.
People call only on God in harm yet later associate partners after receiving favor, directly exposing the instability of the owner's relation to his Lord.
The promise of an eternal tree and a kingdom that will not decay closely parallels the temptation to treat a worldly possession as imperishable.
The question whether wealth and children mean that good is being hastened to people directly challenges the owner's confidence grounded in abundance.
The wrongdoer's wish that he had not taken a destructive companion extends the immediate hand-biting regret that closely parallels the focus.
The admission that a companion diverted one from the reminder explains how regret can culminate in recognizing a fatal misplaced attachment.
Qarun's claim that his wealth was given through his own knowledge supplies a close parallel to possessive confidence in material abundance.
Qarun being swallowed with his dwelling gives a dramatic counterpart to the sudden collapse of wealth and the failure of any supporting group.
Those who had desired Qarun's position reverse their judgment after his fall and recognize God's control over provision, directly correcting wealth-based confidence.
People call sincerely on God in danger but associate partners after rescue, directly clarifying the focus's repudiation of association when loss exposes its error.
Humanity calls upon its Lord in hardship yet a party associates partners after tasting mercy, closely matching the focus's reversal from security to recognition.
A person calls on God in adversity, then forgets Him after favor and sets up equals, directly framing the owner’s belated rejection of association.
The recipient of a favor who claims it came through personal knowledge illustrates the self-attributing confidence that the garden parable overturns.
The soul's cry of regret for neglect toward God gives a direct eschatological counterpart to the owner's lament after irreversible loss.
The recipient of mercy claims it as his own, denies the Hour, and presumes a better return to his Lord, forming a near-conceptual parallel to the garden owner.
Worldly life is likened to vegetation that flourishes, then dries and becomes debris; its wealth and children are explicitly transient adornment.
People who thought their fortified homes would protect them are unexpectedly overtaken by God, a close structural parallel to false security ending in ruin.
The owners of a garden are tested as they plan to harvest it, providing the Qur'an's closest parallel narrative of productive property and moral failure.
Their garden becomes like a harvested ruin overnight, directly paralleling the focus's total loss of fruitful property.
The garden owners confess that they were wrongdoers after seeing the devastation, closely matching the owner's self-reproach and repentance.
Their cry that they were transgressors is a direct collective counterpart to the focus's recognition that his prior stance was wrong.
Their hope that God may give them better than the lost garden and their turning to Him offer the constructive counterpart to the owner's lament.
The hoarder who counts his wealth supplies a close portrait of treating accumulated property as a source of lasting security.
The belief that wealth will make one immortal directly parallels the owner's false assumption that his garden would never perish.
